segments.text: In hardware design, we want a working concept early, and the best feedback is a picture. Ask a frontier model and the picture looks right but doesn't work: four blades on a three-blade design, hoppers that never connect. Feedback fixes one thing and breaks another.

Hardware Engineer is a self-improving engineering team built on Meta models. Give it one paragraph, not a specification. It sets the concept-level requirements itself and returns a concept that works, ready for detail design.

It works like a hardware team. Experts argue on one shared whiteboard. A reviewer checks the design like a senior engineer. A rejection becomes a written gradient that rewrites the team's own instructions, inspired by TextGrad. A picture loop draws and checks the design, and lessons carry to the next problem.

Zoom in. The engineer gives only the what. Four experts and a chief designer search the literature, calculate, simulate and sketch. The reviewer's critique flows back in two steps: what in the design must change, and which instruction let the fault through.

keys.caption: The engineer gives only the what
Experts and a chief designer, one whiteboard
Lessons carry to the next problem

segments.text: A real step. The reviewer rejects the hand truck: the backbone cannot fold into the van, and the bending uses the wrong beam model. The manager writes what must change and why the instructions let it through, then rewrites only those lines. Next meeting, those issues are checked first, and pass.
The whiteboard never resets. Over two meetings it grows from thirty-four sources and twelve calculations to sixty-eight and forty-four, and every claim points to its evidence.

Then the picture. A code sketch fixes the geometry and Muse Image renders it. Meta's models are multimodal, so the critic looks at the picture itself and compares it with the sketch and the design text. A wrong picture is fixed locally; a wrong design goes back to the team.

keys.caption: SAM maps every part, the critic checks
Wrong part: fix it locally, keep or revert
Design flaw: back to the expert team
The final figure, panel by panel

segments.text: Why SAM? Image models miss small parts and, told to fix one, redraw everything. SAM 3.1 gives the critic and the editor each part's exact region. Its numbered marks made the critic count four blades on a three-blade rotor; in the final run it still argued one away.
Here is a robot fingertip. SAM finds the skin, the pillars, the flex circuit, the core and the cable. The figure shows how it works, how it is measured, and how it is made, step by step.
The same team designed an excavator, a turbine, a stair-climbing hand truck, a solar cold room and a footbridge damper.
Two blind judges scored six problems. Against one frontier prompt, it is a tie: Hardware Engineer is ahead on checked numbers and making plans, and behind on pictures.
We built the same system on Meta's open weights, Muse Spark Open and SAM 3, and the designs still come out working.
Instead of hours at the model, you get a stable concept that works, from a team that learns your domain with every design. The engineer gives the what. Hardware Engineer works out the how.
